title: Best Tennis Rackets UK
short: Tennis rackets compared by weight, head size and playing style, from power frames to control frames.
intro: The right tennis racket depends on your level and how you play, not just the brand on the frame. This guide compares rackets reviewed by TennisCompanion, covering power, control, comfort and stability frames so you can match the racket to your game.

products.name: Pure Drive
products.best_for: Beginners to advanced players who want easy power
products.key_spec: 100 sq in head, deflects and transfers energy efficiently
products.summary: A racket that quickly deflects and transfers more energy to the ball, excelling on serves and groundstrokes, though it rates lower for control and feel and its stiffness reduces comfort.
pros: Quickly deflects and transfers energy to the ball

products.name: Pure Aero
products.summary: TennisCompanion calls this a "spin machine" thanks to its aerodynamic design, excellent for groundstrokes and spin generation, though the stiffer frame affects touch shots.
cons: Potential arm discomfort with polyester strings

products.name: Percept 97D
products.best_for: Strong intermediate to advanced all-court players
products.summary: A highly responsive racket with precision ball striking, ideal for net play, though it requires sound technique and doesn't provide easy power.

products.name: Clash 100
products.best_for: Beginners and intermediates, or players with arm concerns
products.summary: An arm-friendly racket with an ultra-low stiffness rating and balanced performance, though it offers lower stability and can be overpowered by heavy pace.

products.name: Blade 98 16x19
products.best_for: Intermediate to advanced players who value touch
products.summary: A braided graphite construction that gives refined control and exceptional net play, though it offers moderately less power and spin than the Pure Drive or Pure Aero.

products.name: Gravity Pro
products.best_for: Strong intermediate to advanced players who face pace
products.summary: A stable racket that handles opponent pace effectively and holds its own at the net, though it offers lower easy power and its weight demands a strong swing.
cons: Heavier weight demands a strong swing

guide.q: What head size should I choose?
guide.a: Larger heads (100 in² and above) give a bigger sweet spot and more easy power, which suits beginners and improvers. Smaller heads (95-98 in²) give more precision and control for players with a more developed technique, at the cost of some forgiveness.

Stiffer rackets transfer more energy into the ball for extra power, but transmit more shock to your arm, which can be uncomfortable or aggravate injuries. More flexible rackets, like the Wilson Clash here, are gentler on the arm but generate less power on their own.

Power rackets suit players who want easy pace with a shorter, more compact swing. Control rackets suit players with a full, fast swing who want precision rather than extra help. All-round or stability rackets aim for a balance between the two.

Heavier rackets tend to feel more stable and absorb pace better, but require a stronger, faster swing to generate power. Lighter rackets are more manoeuvrable and easier to swing quickly, which particularly helps at the net and on serve.
